title: Benchmark Transfer Test: Do Safety Scores on Academic Benchmarks Predict Red-Teaming Success?

original_idea.title: Benchmark Transfer Test: Do Safety Scores on Academic Benchmarks Predict Red-Teaming Success?
original_idea.problem: Academic safety benchmarks and real-world red-teaming may measure different things. It is unknown whether a model's score on AILuminate or TrustLLM predicts its vulnerability to creative red-team attacks.
original_idea.direction: Evaluate 3-4 open-source models on a standard safety benchmark (AILuminate subset). Then conduct a structured red-teaming session using AISafetyLab or manual methods with 20-30 novel attack prompts not in existing benchmarks. Compute rank correlation between benchmark scores and red-teaming success rates. Analyze discrepancies.
original_idea.why_it_matters: If benchmark scores predict red-team vulnerability, benchmarks are valid proxies. If not, the field needs to invest more in adversarial evaluation methods. This is a fundamental validity question.
original_idea.relevant_context: AISafetyLab is listed as a key tool. AILuminate is a key dataset. The relationship between benchmark scores and real-world adversarial robustness has been questioned but not rigorously tested at this scale.

theory_of_impact.reasoning: Strong chain: this is a fundamental validity question for the safety benchmarking enterprise, directly informing whether benchmarks are useful proxies for real-world safety.

accessible_complexity.reasoning: Intermediate: running benchmarks is feasible, but manual red-teaming requires creativity and adversarial thinking skills that may be challenging for beginners.

narrow_scope.reasoning: Sustained effort: running full benchmarks plus conducting structured red-teaming sessions on 3-4 models is substantial work for a 30-hour timeframe.

novelty.reasoning: The predictive validity of safety benchmarks against adversarial red-teaming is a recognized gap. An October 2025 paper from OpenAI/Anthropic/DeepMind showed adaptive attacks achieve >90% success against most published defenses, suggesting a disconnect. RedBench (2025) provides a universal red-teaming dataset. The CAMLIS Red Teaming Report (2025) documents large-scale exercises. However, no published study directly correlates standard benchmark scores (AILuminate, TrustLLM) with structured red-teaming success rates on the same models. The specific correlation methodology is mostly novel.

evidence: Adaptive attacks achieving >90% success on published defenses (Oct 2025, OpenAI/Anthropic/DeepMind)
